commits.author: rjpower
commits.message:
Consolidate agent skills around distinct workflows (#10462)

Reduce the agent skill catalog from 42 entry points to 25 with explicit
ownership boundaries. Make manage-pr the workflow for PR authors,
combine correctness and holistic review under review-pr, and keep
conditional operational procedures as references under their owning
skills.

Move shared writing and experiment-recording guidance into the developer
docs and CI-only procedures beside Loom automation. Preserve review
comment markers, telemetry identities, approval boundaries, and recovery
gates. Keep one canonical incident definition and emit telemetry for the
selected review mode. Scrub procedures register no schedules; recurring
runs require a Loom watch that names the procedure.

When integrating #10422, add its audit-grader skill to the catalog and
point its writing guidance at the developer docs. Whichever PR lands
second needs these updates.

commits.author: ravwojdyla-agent
commits.message:
taskforge: test agentic graders with wrong answers made from the controls (#10445)

After the evidence rules, `submit` now grades wrong answers that it
makes from the agent's two controls. They are the right answer with one
unit more or less in its last digit, the right and the wrong answer as a
list in the two orders, and an empty answer. If the grader accepts one
of them, `submit` refuses the task. The check uses only the task's own
grader, so it does not read the grader spec. In a replay on 373 accepted
tasks, these wrong answers found the same 16 loose tolerances and
substring graders as rules that read the spec, and no other task. When a
version has more than one right control, the one with the fewest
decimals sets the precision: in three runs, 7 of 950 right controls had
more decimals than the reference.

`submit` also refuses CSV files whose rows have different field counts,
invalid JSON files and keyword graders. It refuses a task whose answer a
solver with the prompt alone and no files guesses in at least three of
four attempts, and these guesses use no rollout budget. In a replay on
labeled tasks, the guess check refused 7 of 50 blocking, 2 of 46 ok and
4 of 145 minor tasks.

A review that finds a list of options from which the answer selects one
refuses the task, and the agent prompt states this rule. On 313 labeled
tasks, 27% of the option tasks that a review accepted had a blocking
flaw, against 8% of the other tasks. Rules on the option length and
place were active in that replay and did not close the gap, so they are
not in this PR.

`submit` does not search the prompt and the files for the reference
answer. In seven runs, such a search refused 61 task versions. In about
58 of them, the answer was an ID, a date or a label that the task asks
the solver to find in the data. Among the accepted tasks, it found one
real leak, a format example equal to the answer, and the guess check
refuses that task in 8 of 8 replays.

Part of #10152. Follows #10444.

---------

Co-authored-by: Rafal Wojdyla <ravwojdyla@gmail.com>

[grug] Unroll the EP combine gather-sum over top-k routes (#10346)

`_combine_gather_sum_impl` summed the top-k gathered rows with
`jax.lax.fori_loop` when the Sonic kernel is unavailable, which is the
case without jax_triton (the AMD clusters we use). XLA does not fuse
across loop iterations, so each route reread and rewrote the float32
[tokens, hidden] accumulator. A Python loop over the routes restores the
single fused pass the ring_filtered combine had before it moved into
this shared helper. The Sonic path is unchanged.

June Snowball on one 8x MI355X node (EP8, batch 128, ring_filtered,
save_moe): 2.572 -> 2.442 s per step (-5.1%, two runs each), with
unchanged losses.

Part of #9812.

commits.author: muchanem
commits.message:
[taskforge] Add the JSONL and Finelog ledgers (#10292)

Taskforge records every stage, model call and tool call as a timed
ledger span (#10291). This adds the two backends those spans are written
to. `JsonlLedger` appends a workpiece's spans to
`<root>/<workpiece_id>.jsonl` as each span ends, and
`scripts/ledger_summary.py` totals wall time and tokens per kind and
step over those files. `FinelogLedger` writes the same spans to the
`taskforge.ledger` Finelog table, so runs spread over many Iris tasks
can be queried in one place.

The JSONL file is the authoritative record. Finelog writes are queued
and delivered by a background thread, and a flush can report rows
dropped, so Finelog is telemetry: a failed connection or an unconfirmed
flush is logged and never fails the run. `connect_finelog_ledger` opens
the Finelog client and yields the ledger, or None outside an Iris task.
On exit it flushes the rows and closes the client.

Nothing in this stack writes to Finelog yet. The queue runner adds the
tee that records each span to both backends when it lands.

The live GLM tests that record agent runs to a JSONL ledger come with
this PR. Builds on #10291, which added the span and `Ledger` types;
#10293 builds on it.

commits.author: asartran
commits.message:
[grug] Add a ring_filtered expert-parallel MoE backend (#9880)

Adds `ring_filtered`, an opt-in expert-parallel MoE backend
(`moe_implementation="ring_filtered"`). It sends each token only to the
GPUs that own its experts, where `ring` sends every token to every GPU.
On 8x MI355X with `save_moe` remat, it cuts the June 67B-A2B step from
1.575 s to 1.484 s (13.2% → 14.0% MFU). With `recompute_all` it runs at
about the same speed as `ring_gather_combine` there. It is also faster
on H100, but slower on TPU, so TPU should stay on `ring`. Against
`ragged_all_to_all`, the existing backend that also sends tokens only
where their experts are, it ties on MI355X and is 2-4% faster on H100.

`ring` all-gathers every token to every GPU, and every GPU sends back a
full-size output that gets summed with `psum_scatter`. With top-4 of 256
experts on 8 GPUs, a token's experts sit on 3.3 GPUs on average, so most
of what `ring` moves is never used.

`ring_filtered` does this instead:

1. Each GPU sends each token once to each GPU that owns at least one of
its experts, with an `all_to_all`. A second, small `all_to_all` carries
the router weights and expert ids.
2. The receiving GPU runs its experts and sums each token's expert
outputs, weighted by the router, into one row.
3. A third `all_to_all` sends each row back to where it came from.
4. The token's home GPU adds up the rows it gets back.

Example with 4 GPUs, 2 experts each, top-2, 4 tokens per GPU, and 2
slots per destination:

```
GPU g owns experts E(2g) and E(2g+1). GPU 0's tokens and the experts the router picked:
  a: E2 E3    b: E0 E6    c: E1 E5    d: E3 E7

What GPU 0 sends               to GPU 0   to GPU 1   to GPU 2   to GPU 3
  ring        every token      a b c d    a b c d    a b c d    a b c d    16 rows, 7 used
  ring_filtered  C = 2 per block  b c        a d        c .        b d         8 rows, 7 used
                                                     (. = padding)

On GPU 1 (E2, E3), ring_filtered
  receives one block per GPU  from 0: a d   from 1: f h   from 2: j .   from 3: m o
  groups the rows by expert   E2: a f j o   E3: a d h m
  sums each row's outputs     a' = w(a,E2)*E2(a) + w(a,E3)*E3(a)
  sends rows back             block "from 0" (a' d') goes back to GPU 0

GPU 0 adds the rows that came back for each token:
  a' = from GPU 1    b' = from GPU 0 + 3    c' = from GPU 0 + 2    d' = from GPU 1 + 3
```

At batch 64 each collective moves 537 MB per GPU, against 1,174 MB for
`ring`. The expert MLP is the same as `ring`'s: same capacity rule, same
`_select_local_assignments` (#9928) and `ragged_dot`. Rows are moved
with `ring`'s gather helpers from #9860, so there is no hidden-width
scatter-add in the forward or backward pass. `_combine_gather_sum` moves
from the pooled-wave backend into `ep_common.py` so both backends can
share it.

The new setting is the sender capacity. `all_to_all` needs fixed-size
buffers, so each GPU gets a fixed number of slots per destination:
`pooled_transport_capacity_factor` times the number of tokens it would
send there under uniform routing. This reuses the existing
`fixed_pooled_wave_all_to_all` setting, and `moe_mlp` raises if it is
unset.

If more tokens want a GPU than there are slots, the extra tokens lose
their experts on that GPU, even if those experts have spare capacity. We
call these sender drops. `ring` cannot drop tokens this way. We used
1.1, which gave no sender drops on the June benchmark or with uniform
routing. Routing that piles onto one GPU may need a higher value. The
full-model drop rate on MI350X is 1.00-1.12%, against 0.93-0.99% for
`ring`.

Each row compares `ring_filtered` with the platform's default backend:
`ring_gather_combine` on GPUs and `ring` on TPU.

| Hardware | Workload | Remat | Default | ring_filtered | Change |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 8x MI355X | June model | `save_moe` | 1.575 s | 1.484 s | -5.8% |
| 8x MI355X | June model | `recompute_all` | 1.589 s | 1.582 s | -0.4% |
| 8x MI350X | June model | `save_moe` | 1.730 s | 1.580 s | -8.7% |
| 8x MI350X | June model | `recompute_all` | 1.798 s | 1.688 s | -6.1% |
| 8x H100 | 4-layer model | `save_moe` | 0.588 s | 0.565 s | -4.0% |
| 8x H100 | 4-layer model | `recompute_all` | 0.611 s | 0.577 s | -5.6%
|
| 8x H100 | one MoE layer | | 33.4 ms | 25.6-26.1 ms | -22% to -23% |
| TPU v5p-16 | 4-layer model | `save_moe` | 1.043 s | 1.220 s | +17% |
| TPU v5p-16 | 4-layer model | `recompute_all` | 1.118 s | 1.322 s |
+18% |
| TPU v5p-16 | one MoE layer | | 109.9 ms | 131.6 ms | +20% |
| TPU v6e-8 | one MoE layer | | 106.0 ms | 182.7 ms | +72% |

The June model and 4-layer rows use batch 64 and report the median of
steps 2-19. The 4-layer model is the June model cut down to fit in
memory. The one-layer rows time forward and backward at the batch-64
shapes with uniform routing, median of 20 calls.

On MI355X, both backends ran on the same node with
`gpu_pallas_triton_flash` attention (Vultr jobs 11698 and 11699). The
H100 4-layer rows ran in one job on CoreWeave `cw-rno2a` with
`xla_flash` attention (Iris job
`/dev/bridge-cse-018ox-h100-filtered-vs-ragged`). We have not profiled
why `recompute_all` gains so little there.

On MI350X (jobs 454012 / 454021 and 454022 / 454026), the default
backend also had the ROCm top-k change from #9889, which was not merged.
One `ring_filtered` run (454010) ran out of memory at step 5 because of
allocator fragmentation. Its retry passed, and #9901 fixes the
fragmentation.

Losses match to 5 decimals in the TPU pairs, to within 2e-5 on H100 and
to within 3e-4 on MI355X. We have not profiled the TPU slowdown.

`ragged_all_to_all` also sends each token only to the GPUs that own its
experts, but as one row per (token, expert) pair, sized exactly with a
ragged all-to-all, so it has no padding and no sender drops. Same setups
as above:

| Hardware | Workload | Remat | ragged_all_to_all | ring_filtered |
Change |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 8x MI355X | June model | `recompute_all` | 1.583 s | 1.580 s | -0.2% |
| 8x MI355X | June model | `save_moe` | 1.579 s | 1.489 s | -5.7% |
| 8x H100 | 4-layer model | `recompute_all` | 0.590 s | 0.577 s | -2.2%
|
| 8x H100 | 4-layer model | `save_moe` | 0.590 s | 0.565 s | -4.2% |

The MI355X rows ran both backends on the same node (Vultr jobs 11700 and
11701). The H100 `ragged_all_to_all` runs were a separate job on the
same cluster (`/dev/bridge-cse-018ox-h100-ragged-untagged`).

The `save_moe` rows overstate the gap. `ragged_all_to_all` tags none of
its tensors for `save_moe`, so it recomputes everything under that
setting, and its two remat rows are the same speed. An experiment
outside this PR tagged them: `ragged_all_to_all` then matched
`ring_filtered` on MI355X (1.476 s against 1.482 s, same node, job
11706) and reached 0.582 s on H100, still behind. That version also hit
a non-finite loss at step 5 in one of two H100 runs, so it is not ready
to ship.

On the JAX 0.11.0 ROCm stack these runs used, `ragged_all_to_all` fails
unless
`--xla_gpu_experimental_ragged_all_to_all_use_barrier_with_nccl=false`
is set. With JAX 0.11.1 and the 0.11.1 ROCm plugin it runs without the
flag at the same speed (job 11709).

Correctness checks:

- CPU, f32, 8 shards: outputs and all four gradients match a dense
reference to 1e-5, including with sender drops, receiver drops, uneven
padding and an all-padding batch. They match `ring` whenever nothing is
sender-dropped.
- One full-size layer on 8x H100, against f32 `ring`: outputs and
gradients are within 0.47-0.52%. bf16 `ring` is within 0.50-0.57%,
except for the routing-weight gradient at 5.75%, because `ring` casts
the routing weights to bf16 and `ring_filtered` keeps them in f32.

Part of #9812

commits.author: ravwojdyla-agent
commits.message:
taskforge: Agentic Taskforge flavor (#10444)

Design doc:
https://docs.google.com/document/d/1spGGRyLJAlA22SGKaRLLV3AFPZlPAq7OikT2P8NBWD8

<hr>

Add the Agentic Taskforge flavor, `taskforge.agentic`.
`generate_tasks(idea, n, config)` runs one managed agent (#10264) for a
`CapabilityIdea` (#10265). The agent produces up to `n` `TaskSpec`s and
handles research, program building, and difficulty tuning.[^1] An
example driver is
`experiments/post_training/capability_driven_envs/generate_tasks_agentic.py`.

The agent uses a bubblewrap `LocalMachineFactory` shell with Python,
`taskcompendium`, and `verifyit`, without network access. It has six
tools: `grade`, `rollout`, `web_search`, `web_fetch`, `submit`, and
`finish`. Bubblewrap requires `--container-profile
container_profile_privileged` on Iris. Shell output is capped at 32 KiB
per command. The agent's shell uses `ShellHarness.output_limit_bytes`
and `taskforge.capability` from #10442, which is merged.

`submit` enforces an evidence gate keyed by the `TaskSpec` digest, so
the agent cannot accept its own task. A correct control must pass and a
wrong control must fail. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, without thinking, must
pass 0.1–0.8 of at least eight graded solver rollouts, with at most 25%
format failures. The gate also requires at least four adversary rollouts
with a graded answer. Finally, a GLM reviewer solves the task blind,
reads the task, evidence, and its blind solution, then decides. `finish`
refuses once if fewer than `n` tasks are accepted while more than half
the solver rollouts remain. A session that stops before `finish`
receives a report of the tools.

The tools refuse a task id that is not a file name of at most 128
characters, or that an accepted task already has, when they first read
the task, so that no rollouts go to a task whose outputs the driver
cannot write. `submit` also refuses files in `resources.all`, because
the review reads only `resources.worker`. The driver's agent and solver
models resolve the relay again after a connection error, so a relay that
moved does not end the sessions. The tools also refuse a task that sets
`environment_variables` or `setup_commands`: the engine resolves
`${NAME}` from the host, which holds the driver's keys, and setup
commands can rewrite the files that the review reads. The driver sets no
tool-turn timeout, because one turn can hold several tool calls with
their own deadlines, and the attempt timeout bounds the session. A
solver that runs out of turns, budget or output length fails its run,
and the driver sets the judge temperature (0.7). `grade` records a
control only for a graded answer, so an answer that the answer format
rejects does not satisfy the wrong-control rule. A review takes its two
judge calls from the budget before its first call, so it never stops
after the blind solve.

The solver's ShellSim shell has `python3` with the standard library when
the task's package spec lists PyPI packages, even none. The prompt tells
the agent how to give it, and `example_build.py` sets
`package_spec=PackageSpec(pypi_packages=())`. With no package spec,
`python3` is not found, and the solver is limited to awk and bc
arithmetic. The 30-idea results below come from runs without solver
Python.

Every accepted task runs in ShellSim: `submit` refuses a task with a
shell or files unless its semantics are `shell_simulator`, and only
ShellSim runs those. A task with no shell and no files would need no
machine, but no agent made one in the runs (401 of 401 accepted tasks
were ShellSim tasks). The solver's machine, harness and limits are fixed
in `tools.py`, so these tasks do not train a policy on a real Linux
machine with processes, network or git. Support for `linux_process`
tasks can come later: the TaskSpec contract and RolloutEngine already
run them on Docker, bubblewrap, Daytona, Iris and QEMU, and Taskforge
would need a configurable solver machine factory, semantics that follow
it, and a prompt for that machine.

Across 30 ideas, 20 from the catalog and 10 from `analyze_failed_runs`,
with `n = 4`, the agentic generator accepted 59 tasks. Nine ideas
reached 4/4 and 10 reached 0; each idea below four has a report.[^3] The
staged generator using the same gate accepted 3 of 108 tasks; 77 were
outside the pass-rate band, most of them too easy. Blind verifier agents
rated 8 of the 59 agentic tasks blocking (14%) and found no wrong
reference. GLM request tokens per accepted task were 3.9M for agentic
and 0.9M for staged.[^4]

The full branch, including the staged comparison driver, is #10439. More
`submit` checks and rollout-budget changes follow in #10445 and #10446.
This PR alone was not run.[^2] Part of #10152.

[^1]: Design doc:
https://docs.google.com/document/d/1spGGRyLJAlA22SGKaRLLV3AFPZlPAq7OikT2P8NBWD8
[^2]: In an earlier 30-idea run with the leak and tolerance checks but
without the option rules, guess check, rollout cap, and last-line
regrade, blind verifiers rated 22% of accepted tasks blocking.
[^3]: Outputs:
`s3://marin-us-east-02a/user/rav/projects/taskforge-agentic/` (`l30`,
`l30-d09`, `staged-30c`). Three agentic sessions stopped on model or
tool deadlines during a `cw-us-east-02a` controller outage.
[^4]: The agentic figure sums request tokens across about 125 turns per
session. About 98% are the same prefix sent again. `ChatModel` does not
record cached tokens, so actual compute is lower.

---
[Original
description](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10444#issuecomment-6326215912)

commits.author: muchanem
commits.message:
[taskforge] Add the GLM chat client, agent loop and call recording (#10291)

Every later Taskforge stage calls GLM-5.3 through this layer: proposal
and triage make structured calls, the build stage runs agent sessions,
and validation runs graded RolloutEngine trials. `llm` gains a
`ModelClient.complete` that takes request fields such as `tools`, the
tool loop `run_agent` with RolloutEngine's shell tool and Parallel's web
tools, the RolloutEngine model `GlmRolloutModel`, an on-disk call cache,
and an `LLM_CALL` ledger span for every call, failed calls included.
Call recording needs the ledger's record and span types, so
`ledger/records.py` lands here.

`LLMPolicy` now defaults to GLM-5.3's published sampling (temperature
1.0, top_p 0.95). Callers that build `LLMPolicy()` without a
temperature, such as `generate_tasks.py` on main, move from 0.7 to 1.0.

`GlmRolloutModel` runs rollouts under RolloutEngine's messages trace,
because a validation trial is graded and never trained on. Each turn is
one streamed chat-completions call. The turn carries the reply and the
call's usage with empty token ids and no logprobs, and the engine
charges that usage against the attempt's token budget, which Taskforge
leaves unset. A request that carries token ids (a
`ModelRequest.continuation` or pinned prompt ids) raises
`RolloutContractError` before any call. Rollout turns and agent turns
send a `prompt_cache_key` built from the workpiece, round and step, so
the router keeps one conversation on the node that holds its prefix in
cache.

The client bounds connect and write separately from the read timeout and
expires idle pooled connections after 30 s. A stalled read replaces the
connection pool, at most once per 30 s, so the retry cannot reuse a dead
connection. The old pool closes when the last request streaming on it
ends.

This is the first PR of the Taskforge stack and is based on main. #10292
adds the JSONL and Finelog ledger writers on top of it. The rollout
model's RolloutEngine tests need `spec.draft` and land with the spec
package in #10294.

commits.author: Helw150
commits.message:
[harbor] Match Pi failure markers as complete stderr lines (#10517)

After a process is killed, Bash can echo source code containing Pi’s
authentication and context-limit markers to stderr. Substring matching
then misclassifies the process termination. Match these markers only as
complete lines so the original signal error is preserved.

[Investigation](https://marina.oa.dev/echo/wiki/835).

commits.author: rjpower
commits.message:
[loom] Declare the connector's OAuth clients in the stack (#10533)

The marin-loom stack now declares the remote MCP connector's OAuth
clients under `oauthClients`. Activation passes them to Loom's
`deployment.reconcile` as `oauth_clients`, so nobody has to run `loom
oauth-client add` by hand.

- `claude-ai` accepts claude.ai's callback on both `claude.ai` and
`claude.com`.
- `claude-code` accepts Claude Code's loopback callback on any port.

Both are public clients that prove themselves with PKCE, so the stack
carries no secret. In claude.ai the connector takes client ID
`claude-ai` with a blank secret. claude.ai cannot change a connector's
OAuth settings after it is added, so these ids must never be renamed.
Because the stack prunes, removing a client from it revokes every token
the client was issued. The README's connector section describes this
instead of manual registration.

Depends on marin-community/loom#405. Loom builds without that change
ignore `oauth_clients`, so this config deploys cleanly before it lands
but registers nothing until Loom has the support.

Co-authored-by: rjpower <rjpower@users.noreply.github.com>

commits.author: karansag
commits.message:
[eval] Keep generation overrides out of loglikelihood requests (#10526)

Keep generation budgets and sampling overrides off Evalchemy
loglikelihood requests. Evalchemy c1d5c62c applied `max_gen_toks=256` to
echoed completions, causing lm-eval to score generated tokens along with
the intended continuation. Removing those flags restored Snowball v0.1
BoolQ accuracy from 0.529 to 0.8336 (3,270 items), versus 0.832 on H100;
see the [parity
table](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10270#issuecomment-6326371478).

Add the tested single-host v6e-8 TP8 and v5p-8 TP4 reference configs,
including the explicit 19-local/7-global attention schedule. Their
`layer_types` override is needed until the pinned tpu-inference revision
includes [tpu-inference
#34](https://github.com/marin-community/tpu-inference/pull/34), which
addresses the configuration defect investigated in #10250. The configs
name the staged us-east5 checkpoint and document the tested backend
pins.

Current main already includes the FineStore completion check,
OlympiadBench judge support, and 1,800-second transport attempt timeout;
those remain unchanged, including the total retry budget of three times
the configured timeout.

`host-test-budget uv run --frozen --no-sync pytest
tests/evals/test_evalchemy_config.py -q`: 58 passed. Mechanical
lint/type checks and the lint-catalog review passed. `host-test-budget
uv run --no-project infra/ci/run_tests.py --workers 2 --base-ref
c35dff75fb` was partial: 2,087 passed, 4 skipped, 5 xfailed before the
600-second session limit; the unmarked async test in
`experiments/post_training/capability_driven_envs/tests/test_stage_coordinator.py`
failed identically when run independently from base commit `c35dff75fb`.

Part of #10270.

commits.author: rjpower
commits.message:
[loom] Add the claude profile and enable the claude.ai connector (#10507)

Turn on Loom's claude.ai connector on loom.oa.dev and add the `claude`
launch profile that connector launches use by default. The connector is
a Streamable HTTP MCP endpoint at https://loom.oa.dev/mcp, and Loom is
its OAuth authorization server. Open-Athena members sign in with GitHub,
as in the web UI, and keep access only while their organization lease
keeps renewing.

The profile is named for where the work comes from, not the agent. It
inherits the interactive default, so it runs Codex with the default
model and repository access. Its instructions treat context wrapped from
a claude.ai chat or browser page as data, not instructions. They also
require a pull request labeled `agent-generated` that the agent does not
merge, and they put every created URL in the final status and result,
because the person reads the outcome in claude.ai.

After deploy, a Loom administrator registers claude.ai once with `loom
oauth-client add`, and an organization admin adds the custom connector
in claude.ai. The README section gives both steps. Claude.ai calls
`/mcp`, `/oauth/*` and `/.well-known/oauth-*` from Anthropic's servers,
so those paths must stay publicly reachable.

Deploy this only after marin-community/loom#404 is on Loom's default
branch. An older Loom build rejects the unknown `connector.enabled`
setting, so activation would fail.

[iris] Deliver application secrets through files (#10474)

Deliver application secrets through per-attempt VM tmpfs files and
Pod-owned Kubernetes Secrets. Rigging provides named file-first lookup
with environment fallback and shared native HF and AWS file discovery.
Submissions automatically include the client's current mounted bundle
and available HF/W&B/CoreWeave credentials from files or environment
fallback. Explicit entries override inherited defaults. Other
credentials use the secrets map or CLI `--secret NAME SOURCE`.

The submitting client resolves inheritance for ordinary child jobs, Fray
actors and Zephyr workers. `SecretBehavior.ISOLATE` and sandboxes send
only explicit secrets. The controller receives the resolved map for
dispatch and retries. Remove cluster default application credentials and
operator environment injection. Ordinary `env_vars` retain environment
delivery.

CoreWeave tasks require the submitter's own storage keys, delivered
through the same bundle with native AWS file discovery. Their output
uploader receives only a native AWS file containing the submitted
storage keys. Operator storage keys remain restricted to infrastructure
Pods. Development callers of `configure_coreweave_s3()` must supply
native AWS credential configuration explicitly; it no longer exports
credential values into the process environment. Controller signing
credentials remain controller-only. Submitted values still travel
through authenticated job RPCs and remain in database/checkpoint state;
display APIs redact every secret-map value.

Apply the IaC namespace Role/RoleBinding for per-attempt Secrets before
deploying the Kubernetes controller. The `cw-us-west-04a` stack must
first import CI's bootstrapped `task-secret-role` and
`task-secret-binding` resources into Pulumi state, following the linked
deployment guide. Update submitters and runtime images together, and
roll GCP workers for new attempts to use files. Existing containers
retain their original delivery. No new HF/W&B cloud resources or grants
are required. See the [secret-delivery
guide](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/weaver/rigging-secret-management/lib/iris/docs/secrets.md)
for configuration, deployment and rotation.

commits.author: muchanem
commits.message:
[taskcompendium] Start grading in the grader workspace (#10102)

The grading machine now starts in the grader's workspace unless its
environment specifies a `working_directory`. This restores the behavior
before #10021 when the environment names no directory and preserves an
explicit directory when it does.

Since #10021, every script-graded task has failed while creating its
grading machine on Iris. `_grade_staged` previously passed
`workdir=grading.workspace`; the move to `prepare_machine_spec` dropped
that argument. When the grader environment names no directory,
`prepare_machine_spec` retains the spec's workdir, which is empty for an
image machine because `rolloutengine._machine_spec` leaves it empty.
Docker interprets an empty workdir as the image's `WORKDIR`, so laptop
grading continued to work. Iris instead runs `mkdir -p ""` and fails:

```
RuntimeError: Failed to create Iris workdir : mkdir: cannot create directory ''
```

The Taskforge ladder dry run on cw-rno2a hit this failure in every
grader sandbox. Solver and control machines were unaffected because
`draft.requirements` names `/workspace`.

A test checks the spec passed to the factory with and without an
explicit `working_directory`; the grader-workspace case fails on main.
The ShellSim-backed taskcompendium suite passed locally. The
bubblewrap-backed tests require Linux, and CI runs the full suite.

---

commits.author: bobashopcashier
commits.message:
[levanter] Compute grug cross-entropy gradients in the forward (#10311)

Add an option for grug's cross-entropy to compute its gradients during
the forward pass. The EP hero turns it on with
`ce_grad_in_forward_token_block_size` (or
`--ce-grad-in-forward-token-block-size` in the diagnostic launcher). The
default, `None`, keeps the current `xla_fast_bwd` kernel, and per-token
losses (`reduction="none"`) always use it.

The current kernel runs one matmul in the forward and three in the
backward, because the backward recomputes the logits. When the loss is a
sum or a mean, each token's gradient scale is already known in the
forward. The new path uses that to compute d/dx and d/dw while each
block of logits is still in memory, as Liger-Kernel does. That takes
three matmuls in total, and the backward only rescales the saved
gradients.

Measured on one B200 at the hero's per-GPU shape (65,536 tokens, hidden
6,144, vocab 128,256, bf16) with the new variants in
`bench_ce_hero_shape.py`:

| Path | Value + gradient | Peak HBM |
|---|---|---|
| `xla_fast_bwd` (current) | 351-356 ms | 12.08 GB |
| Gradients in forward, 4,096-row blocks | 242.6 ms | 13.06 GB |

Blocks of 8,192 and 16,384 rows take 252-254 ms. Gradient error against
a float32 reference is unchanged (relative RMS 1.45e-3 for d/dx, 1.43e-3
for d/dw), and the mean loss is within 3.8e-6 of the current path. Peak
memory rises by about 1 GB because the gradients stay in memory from the
forward to the backward.

GB200 runs the current kernel in 310 ms, so the expected saving is about
94 ms per hero step, about 0.7% of a 14 s step. The new path has not run
on GB200 or inside the full hero step.

commits.author: Helw150
commits.message:
[harbor] Exclude inline policy references from the Tau3 prompt (#10405)

Tau³ tasks have two blocks: `<instructions>` tells a standalone coding
agent how to start, advance, and end the conversation; `<policy>`
contains the customer-service rules. Our relay is meant to control the
conversation itself, so it should give the Pi coding agent
relay-specific conversation instructions plus only the domain policy.

The parser includes `<instructions>` in the extracted policy, giving Pi
conflicting directions about who controls the conversation. In the
observed run, Pi ended the conversation, then the relay tried to send
another message and failed.

Extract only the policy block.

Upstream Harbor's [task
template](https://github.com/harbor-framework/harbor/blob/867801035118d1e75c0996821779b59238c7fb29/adapters/tau3-bench/src/tau3_bench/task-template/instruction.md#L1-L16)
has the same structure. Its [reference-agent
extractor](https://github.com/harbor-framework/harbor/blob/867801035118d1e75c0996821779b59238c7fb29/adapters/tau3-bench/tau3_llm_agent.py#L28-L41)
already avoids this bug by selecting the policy block immediately after
`</instructions>`.

[Investigation](https://marina.oa.dev/echo/wiki/810).

commits.author: asartran
commits.message:
[grug] Reorder AMD flash attention launches and retile dK/dV (#10344)

Make the AMD Pallas-Triton flash attention kernels faster by changing
the order in which their programs launch and the tile shape of the dK/dV
kernel. On 8x MI350X, flash attention time per June Snowball step drops
from 245 to 167 ms, and step time drops by 4.3%.

Launch order: with causal or sliding-window masks, some query and key
blocks have much more work than others. Triton launches programs with
the first grid axis varying fastest. The block index was on the first
axis, so blocks of different lengths launched interleaved. It is now on
the last axis, so it varies slowest and the longest blocks for every
batch row and head start first, leaving the short blocks to fill in at
the end. This applies to the forward, dQ and dK/dV kernels. On MI350X
this order alone made each kernel 1.2 to 1.5x faster at 4 to 16
sequences per GPU.

dK/dV tiles: the dK/dV kernel now works on transposed 64x128 tiles (4
warps, 1 stage). In that layout the kernel computes P^T and dS^T
directly, which are the shapes the dV and dK matmuls take. That removes
two in-register transposes per block.

The forward, dQ and dK/dV kernels now share one predicate for the band
mask.

June Snowball on 8x MI350X (EP8, batch 64, ring_dedup, save_moe):

| Metric | Before | After | Change |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Flash attention time per step | 245 ms | 167 ms | -32% |
| Step time | 1.597 s | 1.528 s | -4.3% |
| MFU | 14.15% | 14.80% | +0.65 points |

Loss and peak memory are unchanged. After this change, a sweep of 65
block configurations at batch 16 found no faster tile sizes. The flash
attention tests pass on MI350X.

Part of #9812.

commits.author: dlwh
commits.message:
Support context parallelism in the Hero pipeline (#9283)

Add context parallelism to the Hero pipeline mesh and synthetic runner.
Attention metadata follows query-token sharding, and next-token labels
are formed from global token IDs so a context slice can target the first
token in the next slice. Batch divisibility excludes context replicas.
Require Flash Attention 4 beta 28 or later for the pipeline environment.

Target main directly: #9119, #9282, and #9279 (including #9278) are
merged. The CP adaptation now lives in
experiments/grug/moe_hero_pipeline and preserves the merged pipeline's
optimizer, checkpoint, and runtime controls. The previous
dependency-only integration branch is no longer required.

The historical 535B, 48-layer model completed ten finite synthetic
updates on 192 H100s with PP24 × EP4 × CP2, sequence length 65,536,
batch 96, and 24 microbatches: 6,291,456 tokens per update. Median step
time was 68.539 seconds, measured MFU was 9.877%, and loss went from
11.792197 to 11.449181. All 24 workers exited successfully. Gate 06
launched c55ab40a29 with helper dependency overrides; 3ad8d3ce37
subsequently recorded those dependencies. These measurements predate the
refresh onto main; the refreshed integration has not been rerun on GPUs.
Detailed evidence is in #9277.

The historical run required scratch JAXPP overlays for host-memory mesh
rebinding, forward activation-offload placement, and Dime2 send-buffer
lifetime. It retained disposable warmup, host parking of model state,
and CUDA synchronization after each step. The required JAXPP overlays
are external to this PR and block a stock-install reproduction; the
synchronization workaround's root cause remains unresolved. The two-CPU
regression compares CP2 staged loss and every gradient against the CP1
unsplit model at unchanged tolerances; it does not validate JAXPP MPMD
communication or GPU kernels.
